exercise.title: Why do trigonometric integrals begin by saving a differential?

statement.p: For powers of sine and cosine, the book saves one factor that becomes du and rewrites the rest with an identity. In your own words, why is the saved piece the one that matches the derivative of the other trigonometric function, rather than a factor chosen at random?

hint.p: Substitution needs du to appear. The derivative of \sin x is \cos x, and the derivative of \cos x is -\sin x, so those factors are the natural differentials.

cell.p: Save one \cos x\,dx, convert remaining cosines using \cos^2x=1-\sin^2x.
Save one \sin x\,dx, convert remaining sines using \sin^2x=1-\cos^2x.

paragraphs.p: The point is not the table. The point is the saved differential. We save the piece that matches the derivative of the other trigonometric function.

subsection.title: Powers of tangent and secant
subsection.p: Again, we try to save a differential.

paragraphs.title: An even power of secant
paragraphs.p: If the power of \sec x is a positive even integer (at least 2), save one factor of \sec^2 x\,dx. Then convert the remaining powers of secant into tangent.

exercise.title: What derivative pairs guide tangent-secant integrals?

statement.p: The useful pairs are \frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x and \frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x. In your own words, why do you look for \sec^2 x\,dx or \sec x\tan x\,dx as a saved differential, and how does \sec^2 x=1+\tan^2 x finish the rewrite?

hint.p: Same habit as sine and cosine: save the factor that is a derivative, then use the Pythagorean identity to express what remains in the substitution variable.

subsection.title: Product-to-sum identities
subsection.p: do not fit the power patterns above. The angles are different. In this case, product-to-sum identities turn products into sums, and sums are easier to integrate.

exercise.title: Why do different angles want product-to-sum identities?

statement.p: A product such as \sin(5x)\cos(2x) does not fit the power patterns. In your own words, why do identities that turn products into sums make the integral easier, and why is that still a structural response rather than a new kind of calculus?

hint.p: Sums of sines and cosines integrate term by term. The identities are algebra that reveals those sums; the integration step is then ordinary.

example.title: Example
example.p: The identity did the hard work. Once the product became a sum, the integral was routine.

exercise.title: Why is an odd power more helpful than two even powers?

statement.p: An odd power of cosine lets you save \cos x\,dx and convert the rest by \cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x. In your own words, why does that strategy fail when both powers are even, and why do half-angle identities appear in that case?

hint.p: If a sine or cosine power is odd, saving one factor leaves an even power of that same function, which the Pythagorean identity converts into the other function. If both powers are even, half-angle identities lower the powers instead.
